- When sentiment is negative (e.g., -1.00) or shows strong bearish momentum, model tends to overcorrect downward — reduce forecasted drop magnitude or add slight upward bias to avoid excessive sell-off.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior period), model often overshoots downward in next period — cap forecast decline or adjust downward only if sentiment remains neutral or bullish.
- If sentiment is positive (e.g., 1.00) and price is falling, model often underreacts — increase forecasted rebound or add early mean-reversion bias to avoid missing reversal.
- Model consistently underestimates true price decline in early 2024 (e.g., 2024-01-23) — apply a 2–5% upward bias to forecast for first 3–5 days post-spike.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed, model tends to overfit recent volatility — smooth forecast curve using 3–5 day moving average to reduce noise.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 2024-01-23: 63.27 → 65.80 → 63.41), model often fails to recognize it — add a 1–3 day lagged mean-reversion term to forecast.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates volatility in early periods — reduce forecast variance by 15–20% if sentiment is weak or neutral.
